question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The patient remembers his son taking him to the temple.
option_1: The patient remembers he was taken to the temple by his son.
option_2: The patient remembers taken to the temple by his son.
option_3: The patient remembers himself being taken to the temple by his son.
option_4: The patient remembers being taken to the temple by his son.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The patient remembers being taken to the temple by his son.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The patient remembers his son taking him to the temple" uses the structure remembers + subject + gerund (V-ing) + object, where the son is the doer of the action "taking" and the patient (referred to as "him") is the receiver of the action.

• Rule — Passivising a gerund clause after verbs like "remember/recall":
◦ Active: Subject1 + remembers + Subject2 + V-ing + Object (=Subject1)
◦ Passive: Subject1 + remembers + being + V3 + by + Subject2

• Applying the rule: "his son taking him" becomes "being taken ... by his son". Since the object of "taking" (him) is the same person as the one who "remembers", it is simply dropped and understood, giving the natural passive form "The patient remembers being taken to the temple by his son."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it changes the sentence into a finite clause ("he was taken"), which alters the original non-finite gerund construction and changes the meaning/structure of what is remembered.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "remembers taken" is grammatically incomplete — it is missing the auxiliary "being", without which the passive gerund form cannot be formed.

• Option 3 is incorrect because inserting the reflexive pronoun "himself" is redundant here — since the person taken and the person who remembers are already understood to be the same (the patient), "himself" is unnecessary and makes the sentence unidiomatic.

NOTE

• Verbs like remember, recall, recollect, enjoy, avoid, admit, deny are commonly followed by a gerund (V-ing) in active voice, whose passive form uses being + V3.

• Example: Active — "I remember my teacher scolding me." Passive — "I remember being scolded by my teacher."

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Formal forgiveness of a person’s sins
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Absolution.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Absolution" means the formal, official forgiveness of a person's sins, typically granted by a priest or a religious authority. (औपचारिक क्षमा/पाप-मुक्ति)
◦ Example: The priest granted the dying man absolution for his sins.

• The word comes from the Latin "absolvere", meaning "to set free" or "to acquit".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Ablutions (स्नान/शुद्धिकरण की क्रिया): The act of washing oneself, especially as part of a religious ritual — this refers to physical cleansing, not the forgiveness of sins.

• Option 3: Absolutism (निरंकुशता): A political system in which one ruler or authority has complete, unrestricted power — unrelated to forgiveness.

• Option 4: Forgiveness (क्षमा): A general, everyday word for pardoning someone; it lacks the specific formal/religious sense required by the given definition, so it is too generic to be the precise one-word substitute being tested here.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused "formal pardon/release" one-word substitutes for SSC: Amnesty (a general pardon for political offences), Reprieve (postponement of a punishment), Exoneration (clearing someone of blame).

• Do not confuse Absolution (forgiveness of sin) with Resolution (a firm decision) or Dissolution (breaking up/ending).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
It is undesirable to invest a part of your earnings for future use.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. advisable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Undesirable" means not wanted, unpleasant, or not recommended. (अवांछनीय/अनुचित)

• Its antonym, "advisable", means worth doing, recommended, or sensible/prudent, i.e. exactly the opposite sense that fits the sentence once reversed — it becomes sensible/recommended to invest a part of one's earnings. (उचित/सलाह देने योग्य)
◦ Example: It is advisable to save a portion of your salary every month.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: foolish (मूर्खतापूर्ण): Means unwise or lacking good sense — this is close in meaning to "undesirable/unwise", not its opposite.

• Option 3: unadvisable: This is simply a negative of "advisable" and carries almost the same sense as "undesirable" itself (not recommended), so it is a near-synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 4: meek (विनम्र/नम्र): Means quiet, humble and easily imposed upon — it describes a personality trait and has no direct relation to "desirable/undesirable".

NOTE

• Common antonym pairs tested by SSC around this word family: desirable ⟷ undesirable, advisable ⟷ inadvisable, favourable ⟷ unfavourable, feasible ⟷ infeasible.

• Remember: "un-" and "in-"/"-able" prefixes/suffixes often form direct opposites in English (e.g., desirable/undesirable), so always check whether the option is simply a negated form of the same root (a synonym) rather than a genuine antonym.

question: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition.
option_1: Ashok was in the bus stop.
option_2: Ashok was to the bus stop.
option_3: Ashok was on the bus stop.
option_4: Ashok was at the bus stop.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Ashok was at the bus stop.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Preposition "at" for a point/location: We use "at" to refer to a specific point or place, such as a bus stop, a crossing, a particular building, or an address, when we are simply indicating presence at that point.
◦ Example: The children were waiting at the bus stop.

• A "bus stop" is treated as a point location (a specific spot), not an enclosed space (which would need "in") or a flat/elevated surface (which would need "on"), so "at" is the only preposition that fits idiomatically.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "in" is used for enclosed spaces or areas with boundaries (e.g., "in the room", "in the city") — a bus stop is not an enclosed space.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "to" indicates movement/direction towards a place (e.g., "He went to the bus stop"), not a state of being present there ("was to" is ungrammatical).

• Option 3 is incorrect because "on" is used for surfaces (e.g., "on the table", "on the road") — a person is not "on" a bus stop the way one is "on" a surface.

NOTE

• Commonly confused prepositions of place for SSC: at the corner / in the corner (of a room) / on the corner (of a street), and at home, in a country/city, on a street.

• General rule of thumb: "at" = point, "in" = enclosed area, "on" = surface/line.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.
The MD of the company let the cat out of the bag by telling her secretary, who got the much coveted promotion.
option_3: To allow a secret to be known, usually without intending to
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To allow a secret to be known, usually without intending to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "let the cat out of the bag" means to reveal a secret carelessly or accidentally, usually without meaning to. (अनजाने में राज़ खोल देना)
◦ Example: He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party before we could stop him.

• The idiom is believed to originate from old market trickery, where a dishonest seller would substitute a cat for a piglet inside a bag — if the cat was let out, the fraud was revealed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: openly confess: This suggests a deliberate, willing admission, whereas the idiom specifically implies an unintentional or careless disclosure — not the same sense.

• Option 2: Creating a false story: This is the opposite idea — the idiom is about revealing a true secret, not inventing a false one.

• Option 4: secretly confide: This suggests a controlled, deliberate, private disclosure to one person, whereas the idiom implies an accidental slip that becomes generally known.

NOTE

• Other common "secret/reveal" idioms for SSC: "spill the beans" (to reveal secret information, usually deliberately or carelessly), "blow the whistle" (to report wrongdoing), "in the loop" (informed about something), "under wraps" (kept secret).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Construction plays a central role in transforming the natural environment into the built environment, and many considerations and restrictions can apply before a project is given consent to proceed in terms of how it may influence the environment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Interdiction.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Consent" means permission or agreement for something to happen. (सहमति/अनुमति)

• "Interdiction" means an official or authoritative prohibition or restraint, i.e. the formal act of forbidding something — the direct opposite of granting permission. (औपचारिक निषेध/रोक)
◦ Example: The court issued an interdiction against the sale of the disputed land.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Bickering (नोक-झोंक): Means a petty, quarrelsome argument — unrelated to giving or refusing permission.

• Option 2: Expulsion (निष्कासन): Means being formally forced out or dismissed from a place or organisation — a different concept from withholding consent.

• Option 3: Directive (निर्देश): Means an official instruction or order telling someone what to do — this is actually closer to authorising/instructing than to refusing permission, so it does not work as an antonym of "consent".

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs of "consent" often tested by SSC: consent ⟷ refusal, consent ⟷ dissent, consent ⟷ prohibition/veto.

• Remember the prefix "inter-" in "interdiction" here comes from Latin "interdicere" (to forbid), not to be confused with "inter-" meaning "between" in words like international.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A great transition / marked / the 20th century / for mankind
option_1: A great transition marked the 20th century for mankind.
option_2: The 20th century marked a great transition for mankind.
option_3: A great transition for mankind marked the 20th century.
option_4: For mankind, a great transition marked the 20th century.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The 20th century marked a great transition for mankind.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In a Subject-Verb-Object sentence, the subject must logically be the one performing the action of the verb. Here the verb is "marked", meaning "represented/signified".

• It is the time period ("the 20th century") that logically "marks" or represents a great transition — not the other way round — so "the 20th century" must be the subject, followed by the verb "marked", then the object "a great transition", and finally the modifying phrase "for mankind".
◦ Correct structure: Subject (the 20th century) + Verb (marked) + Object (a great transition) + Phrase (for mankind).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it makes "a great transition" the subject of "marked the 20th century", reversing the logical relationship — a transition does not "mark" a century in the intended sense of the original idea.

• Option 3 is incorrect for the same reason — "a great transition for mankind" is made the subject, which awkwardly reverses which noun is doing the "marking".

• Option 4 is incorrect because fronting "For mankind" as a dangling introductory phrase, followed by "a great transition marked the 20th century", again wrongly makes the transition the subject and produces an unnatural sentence order.

NOTE

• In parts-rearrangement questions, first identify the main verb and ask which noun phrase can logically and grammatically be its subject — this quickly eliminates most wrong options.

• Time-period subjects (a century/an era/a year) commonly pair with verbs like "marked", "witnessed", "saw", "brought" in SSC sentence-formation questions.

question:
In the given sentence the underlined word may have been incorrectly spelt. Identify the option that rectifies the spelling. If there is no error in spelling, select ‘No error’.
During my time-taking and gradual convaelescenc after my back injury, my family was by my side.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. convalescence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Convalescence" — the process of recovering health and strength gradually after an illness or injury. (स्वास्थ्य-लाभ/रोगमुक्ति की प्रक्रिया)
◦ Example: She spent a long convalescence at her parents' home after the surgery.

• Spelling key: CON + VAL + ESCENCE. Note the sequence "vale" (not "vael"), and the ending "-escence" (as in adolescence, obsolescence) — not "-escenc" or "-esaence".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "convalesaence" — incorrect; the "sa" in the middle is wrong, it should be "sce" (convale-sce-nce).

• Option 2: "No error" — incorrect; the underlined word "convaelescenc" as printed is genuinely misspelt (letters "ae" are transposed and the final "e" is missing), so an error does exist.

• Option 3: "convalecense" — incorrect; it drops one "s" and wrongly ends in "-ense" instead of the correct "-escence".

NOTE

• Other "-escence" ending words commonly tested by SSC: adolescence, obsolescence, effervescence, luminescence, acquiescence.

• The related adjective is convalescent (a person recovering from illness), and the verb form is convalesce.

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct collocation.
Brady straightened, the ________ baton in hand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. wooden.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "baton" (a short, solid stick-like object carried in the hand, as by a marshal, conductor, or officer) is conventionally described by the material it is made of, and "wooden baton" is the natural, commonly used collocation in English for such a hand-held stick.

• Rule — Collocation: Certain adjectives habitually pair with certain nouns purely by convention/usage (not by strict grammar), and a native-sounding sentence must use the word that customarily "collocates" with the noun — here, "baton" collocates naturally with a material-describing adjective like "wooden".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: charge — "charge baton" is not an established English collocation and does not fit naturally before "baton in hand".

• Option 3: swing — "swing" is normally a verb describing the motion of using a baton (to swing a baton), not an adjective describing the baton itself held "in hand"; "swing baton" is not a standard descriptive collocation here.

• Option 4: open — "open baton" does not make sense, as a baton is a solid rod and cannot logically be described as "open".

NOTE

• Collocation questions test which word combination "sounds right" to a native speaker; when unsure, eliminate options that are grammatically odd (like using a verb "swing" as a plain adjective) or semantically impossible (like "open" for a solid object).

• Other commonly tested SSC collocations: heavy rain (not "strong rain"), make a decision (not "do a decision"), strong coffee (not "powerful coffee").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Take something at face value
option_1: Accept something as it looks without thinking about whether it might, in fact, not be quite what it appears
option_2: According to the appearance of something
option_3: Not laugh or change your expression even though you want to laugh
option_4: Show that you do not like something by making an unpleasant expression
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Accept something as it looks without thinking about whether it might, in fact, not be quite what it appears.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "take something at face value" means to accept something exactly as it appears on the surface, without questioning whether there is a deeper or different truth behind it. (जो दिखे उसे वैसा ही मान लेना, बिना गहराई से जाँचे)
◦ Example: Don't take his apology at face value — he has lied to you before.

• The phrase originally comes from the world of currency, where the "face value" of a coin or note is the value printed/stamped on it, regardless of its actual worth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: According to the appearance of something: This is only a partial, literal paraphrase of "face value" and misses the essential idea of "accepting without questioning" that the idiom conveys.

• Option 3: Not laugh or change your expression even though you want to laugh: This is actually the meaning of a different idiom, "keep a straight face", not "take something at face value".

• Option 4: Show that you do not like something by making an unpleasant expression: This describes making a "face" (grimace), which is unrelated to the idiom being tested.

NOTE

• Do not confuse idioms containing the word "face": "face value" (accept as it appears), "keep a straight face" (not show amusement), "lose face" (be humiliated), "save face" (avoid humiliation), "in the face of" (despite/when confronted with).

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
The secretary assures the audience that he/she is going to help them.
option_1: The secretary said to the audience, “I am going to help you.”
option_2: The secretary says to the audience, “I am going to help you.”
option_3: The secretary says to the audience, “I was going to help you.”
option_4: The secretary says to the audience, “I will be going to help you.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The secretary says to the audience, "I am going to help you."

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Reporting verb in the Present Tense: When the reporting verb of the indirect sentence is in the present tense ("assures"), no backshift of tense is required while converting to direct speech — the tense inside the quotation marks stays exactly as it is in the indirect sentence.

• Applying the rule: "assures" (present tense) → reporting verb becomes "says"; "is going to help them" stays as "is going to help you", with the pronoun "them" changing to "you" since we are now quoting the secretary's own words to the audience directly, and "he/she" becomes "I".
◦ Direct: The secretary says to the audience, "I am going to help you."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it uses the reporting verb "said" (past tense), which wrongly implies the indirect sentence was in the past tense, when in fact the given indirect sentence uses the present tense "assures".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it changes the tense inside the quotation marks to "was going to help you" (past), when no backshift is needed as the reporting verb is in the present tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it changes the tense inside the quotation marks to the future continuous-related "will be going to help you", which does not match the original "is going to help them".

NOTE

• When converting indirect to direct speech, always check the tense of the reporting verb first: present/future reporting verb → no backshift; past reporting verb → backshift is reversed to restore the direct (original) tense.

• Pronouns must also be adjusted to match who is actually speaking and who is being addressed in the direct quotation.

question:
Select the correct active form of the given sentence.
My cafe has been revisited by many tourists.
option_2: Many tourists did revisited my cafe.
option_3: Many tourists have revisited my cafe.
option_4: Many tourists has revisited my cafe.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Many tourists have revisited my cafe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "My cafe has been revisited by many tourists" is in the Present Perfect Tense, Passive Voice.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "many tourists" (plural) becomes the subject, so the auxiliary must be "have" (not "has", which is only for singular/third-person-singular subjects); the past participle "revisited" is retained as the main verb, and "my cafe" becomes the object.
◦ Active: Many tourists have revisited my cafe.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "revisited" alone (Simple Past form) is used without the auxiliary "have", which changes the tense from Present Perfect to Simple Past — not equivalent to the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "did revisited" is grammatically wrong — "did" must be followed by the base form of the verb (V1), i.e. "did revisit", not the past participle "revisited"; also, "did" wrongly signals Simple Past instead of Present Perfect.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has" is a singular auxiliary and cannot be used with the plural subject "many tourists" — it should be "have" for agreement.

NOTE

• Subject-verb agreement rule: plural subjects take "have", singular (he/she/it/singular noun) subjects take "has", in the Present Perfect Tense.

• When converting passive to active, the "by + agent" phrase of the passive sentence becomes the subject of the active sentence, and the original subject becomes the object.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The actor was ridiculed for her nonchalant attitude towards her work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Considerate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Nonchalant" means casually calm and relaxed, showing a careless lack of concern or interest. (उदासीन/लापरवाह)

• "Considerate" means careful and thoughtful about the needs and feelings of others/one's responsibilities, i.e. showing genuine care and attentiveness — the opposite of a careless, unconcerned attitude. (विचारशील/सावधान)
◦ Example: Unlike her earlier nonchalant approach, she became far more considerate about her duties at work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Boisterous (उत्साही/शोरगुल वाला): Means noisy, energetic and full of high spirits — this describes a manner of behaving loudly, not the level of care or concern shown towards one's work, so it is not the antonym being tested here.

• Option 2: Unconcerned: This is actually a synonym of "nonchalant" (both mean showing no interest or worry), not its antonym.

• Option 4: Retrospective (पूर्वव्यापी): Means looking back on or dealing with past events — this is unrelated to the idea of being careless versus attentive.

NOTE

• Other words in the "nonchalant/indifferent" family often tested by SSC: casual, apathetic, blasé, insouciant — their antonyms include earnest, attentive, conscientious, considerate.

• Be careful in antonym questions to eliminate options that are actually synonyms in disguise (like "Unconcerned" here) before picking the genuine opposite.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Pacify
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Aggravate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Pacify" means to calm someone down or to bring an end to conflict/anger. (शांत करना)

• "Aggravate" means to make a situation, problem, or someone's anger worse or more serious — the direct opposite of calming something down. (और बिगाड़ना/भड़काना)
◦ Example: His careless remark only aggravated her anger instead of calming her down.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Placate (मनाना/शांत करना): Means to calm or soothe someone's anger — this is a synonym of "pacify", not its antonym.

• Option 2: Assuage (कम करना/शांत करना): Means to ease or lessen a painful or unpleasant feeling — again a synonym of "pacify".

• Option 4: Quell (दबाना/शांत करना): Means to put an end to or suppress something (e.g., quell a riot) — this too is close in meaning to "pacify", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "pacify" frequently tested together by SSC: placate, appease, assuage, mollify, soothe, quell.

• Other antonym options for "pacify" that may appear: provoke, incite, agitate, inflame — all mean to stir up anger or conflict.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Kemp's ridleys are
P. usually found in nearshore and
Q. inshore waters of the northern
R. Gulf of Mexico, especially in Louisiana waters,
S. which are their primary feeding grounds
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. PQRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The base sentence starts with "Kemp's ridleys are", which requires a predicate describing where they are usually found, so the sentence must begin with part P ("usually found in nearshore and"), directly completing the verb "are".

• Following P, the phrase must continue with Q ("inshore waters of the northern"), since "nearshore and inshore waters" is a natural paired phrase, followed logically by the location description R ("Gulf of Mexico, especially in Louisiana waters,"), and the sentence is finally completed by the relative clause S ("which are their primary feeding grounds"), which refers back to "waters".
◦ Correct sentence: "Kemp's ridleys are usually found in nearshore and inshore waters of the northern Gulf of Mexico, especially in Louisiana waters, which are their primary feeding grounds."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (SRQP) is incorrect because it begins with S, whose relative pronoun "which" needs an antecedent noun (like "waters") that has not yet been introduced — S cannot logically come first.

• Option 2 (QPSR) is incorrect because it places Q immediately after the base sentence, but "Kemp's ridleys are inshore waters..." does not make grammatical sense — the predicate must begin with "usually found in..." (P), not with "inshore waters" (Q).

• Option 4 (PRSQ) is incorrect because after P it jumps to R ("Gulf of Mexico...") before Q ("inshore waters of the northern"), breaking the natural phrase "nearshore and inshore waters of the northern Gulf of Mexico" and leaving "northern" disconnected from "Gulf of Mexico".

NOTE

• In parajumble/parts-rearrangement questions, look for a part that must immediately follow the given opening words (here, the verb "are" needs a predicate) and look for natural collocations (like "nearshore and inshore waters") to lock adjacent parts together.

• Relative clauses beginning with "which/who/that" almost always come after the noun they describe, never at the very start of the arrangement.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
A faint mist _________ over the valley.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. hung.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "hung" (past tense of "hang") is the idiomatic word used to describe mist, smoke, fog, or a cloud remaining suspended motionlessly in the air over a place.
◦ Example: A thick fog hung over the city all morning.

• This is a fixed, natural collocation in English — mist/fog/smoke "hangs" over a place, describing something suspended without visible support, which matches the still, floating nature of a faint mist.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: swung — "swing" describes a back-and-forth pendulum-like motion (e.g., a swinging door or pendulum), which does not describe how mist settles over a valley.

• Option 3: swayed — "sway" describes a gentle side-to-side rocking motion (e.g., trees swaying in the wind), which is not the natural verb used for stationary mist.

• Option 4: dangled — "dangle" describes something hanging loosely and swinging freely from a fixed point (e.g., a dangling key chain), which does not fit the image of mist spread over a valley.

NOTE

• Weather-related collocations frequently tested by SSC: mist/fog hangs over, clouds gather, rain pours down, wind whistles through, thunder rumbles/roars.

• "Hang" in the sense of "remain suspended in the air" is distinct from "hang" meaning "to execute by hanging" (past tense: hanged) — SSC sometimes tests this distinction separately.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
She said to me, “You will speak at the conference tomorrow.”
option_1: She told me that I would speak at the conference that day.
option_2: She told me that I might speak at the conference the next day.
option_3: She told me that I will speak at the conference the today.
option_4: She told me that I would speak at the conference the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. She told me that I would speak at the conference the next day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Reporting verb "said to" + past tense reporting verb: When the reporting verb is in the past tense and is of the form "said to [person]", it changes to "told [person]" in indirect speech, and a connector "that" is added.

• Rule — Backshift of tense and time-word change: Since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, the tense inside the quotes is shifted back: "will" → "would"; and the time expression "tomorrow" → "the next day" (as the reference point of "tomorrow" shifts along with the reporting time); the pronoun "you" becomes "I" since she is speaking to "me".
◦ Indirect: She told me that I would speak at the conference the next day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it changes "tomorrow" to "that day" instead of the correct "the next day" — "that day" would be the correct shift for "today", not "tomorrow".

• Option 2 is incorrect because it changes "will" to "might", but "might" is the backshifted form of "may" (possibility), not of "will" (a plain future statement) — this incorrectly alters the meaning from certainty to mere possibility.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it keeps the reporting verb structure "will" unchanged (no backshift) despite "said" being in the past tense, and also uses the phrase "the today", which is not correct English.

NOTE

• Standard time-word shifts for indirect speech: today → that day; tomorrow → the next day/the following day; yesterday → the previous day/the day before; now → then; here → there.

• Standard modal backshifts: will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to/must (unchanged for strong obligation).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Discusion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Discussion" — a conversation or debate about a particular topic. It requires a double "s" in the middle: dis + cuss + ion.

• As printed, "Discusion" is missing one "s" (it should be "Discussion"), which makes it the incorrectly spelt word among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Languish" is correctly spelt — it means to remain in a state of weakness, decline, or neglect.

• Option 2: "Altitude" is correctly spelt — it means the height of an object or point above sea level or ground level.

• Option 4: "Longitudinal" is correctly spelt — it means relating to length, or relating to lines of longitude.

NOTE

• Other commonly misspelt double-consonant words tested by SSC: occurrence, embarrassment, committee, professional, necessary, accommodate, recommend.

• A quick check for "-ssion/-tion" words: verbs ending in a stressed "-cuss/-mit/-fer" type sound often double the consonant before adding "-ion" (discuss → discussion; permit → permission).

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. It not only distances the addict from his/her social circles but also impacts their productivity badly.
B. People begin drinking just for the sake of it and gradually make it a habit.
C. Addiction of any kind, including alcoholic addiction impacts all aspects of an individual’s life.
D. Once it becomes a habit, it does not require much to change into an addiction.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BDCA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The paragraph must begin with a sentence that does not depend on an earlier pronoun reference. Sentence B ("People begin drinking just for the sake of it and gradually make it a habit") introduces the topic (drinking) without needing any prior context, so it must come first.

• Sentence D ("Once it becomes a habit, it does not require much to change into an addiction") logically follows B, since "it" in D refers back to the "habit" of drinking mentioned in B, continuing the drinking → habit → addiction progression.

• Sentence C ("Addiction of any kind, including alcoholic addiction, impacts all aspects of an individual's life") follows next as a general statement once "addiction" has been reached in D, broadening the point from the specific case of drinking to addiction in general.

• Finally, sentence A ("It not only distances the addict from his/her social circles but also impacts their productivity badly") follows C, since "It" in A refers back to the "addiction" introduced in C, and A elaborates on the specific ways addiction impacts life mentioned generally in C.
◦ Correct order: B → D → C → A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BDAC) is incorrect because it places A (which uses "it" to refer to "addiction") before C (which is where "addiction" as a general concept is actually introduced) — the pronoun in A would have no clear antecedent yet.

• Option 2 (DBCA) is incorrect because it starts with D, whose opening phrase "Once it becomes a habit" uses the pronoun "it" without any antecedent having been established first.

• Option 4 (ACBD) is incorrect because it starts with A, whose pronoun "It" again has no antecedent at the very start of the paragraph.

NOTE

• In paragraph (para-jumble) questions, always scan for pronouns like "it/this/that/they" at the start of each sentence — a sentence that opens with such a pronoun almost never begins the paragraph, since its antecedent must be established earlier.

• Look for a natural cause-and-effect or chronological chain (here: drinking → habit → addiction → its effects) to help lock the sequence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
He is in debt due to his judicious tastes and habits.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. extravagant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Judicious" means having or showing good sense and sound judgement, i.e. sensible and prudent — this word logically contradicts the rest of the sentence, since being sensible would not cause someone to fall into debt.

• The sentence needs a word whose meaning is consistent with being in debt: "extravagant" means spending much more money or resources than is necessary or wise, which correctly explains why the person is in debt. (फिजूलखर्च)
◦ Example: He is in debt due to his extravagant tastes and habits.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: affluent (धनी/समृद्ध): Means wealthy or having a great deal of money — this describes a state of being rich, not a habit of spending, and would not by itself explain being in debt.

• Option 2: frugal (मितव्ययी): Means careful with money, avoiding waste — this is the opposite of a habit that would cause debt, so it does not fit the sentence's logic either.

• Option 4: moderate (संतुलित): Means average or not extreme — a "moderate" habit would not typically be severe enough to be singled out as the cause of falling into debt.

NOTE

• In "substitute the underlined segment" questions, first check whether the underlined word makes logical sense in context; if it contradicts the rest of the sentence (as "judicious" does here with "in debt"), the correct substitute must restore logical consistency.

• Related words for "extravagant" often tested by SSC: lavish, wasteful, profligate, spendthrift — their opposites include frugal, thrifty, economical, prudent.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The British king, Charles I, had (1)_________ a very difficult financial situation from his father. His period saw a very high rate of inflation. He wanted to (2)_________ money. Therefore, he (3)_________ creating the title of Baronet and selling it to (4)_________ candidates. However, his decision was (5)_________ by the British parliament.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. inherited.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes a financial situation that Charles I received from his father, upon becoming king — this is precisely the meaning of "inherited", i.e. to receive money, property, a title, or (as here) a situation/problem from a predecessor, typically a parent.

• Rule — contextual word choice: The phrase "from his father" is the key clue; only a word meaning "received from a predecessor" logically completes the sentence "had ___ a very difficult financial situation from his father."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: owned — "owned a difficult financial situation from his father" is not idiomatic; "own" is used for possessing property/objects, not for receiving an abstract situation from someone else.

• Option 3: devised — means to plan or invent something; a king does not "devise" a difficult financial situation from his father, since he did not create the problem himself.

• Option 4: genetic — is an adjective (relating to genes/heredity), not a verb, and cannot grammatically follow "had" in this sentence structure.

NOTE

• "Inherit" is used both literally (property, money, a title) and figuratively (a problem, a situation, a tradition) being passed down from a predecessor — both senses are common in SSC comprehension passages.

• Related word: "inheritance" (noun) — what is inherited; "heir" — the person who inherits.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The British king, Charles I, had (1)_________ a very difficult financial situation from his father. His period saw a very high rate of inflation. He wanted to (2)_________ money. Therefore, he (3)_________ creating the title of Baronet and selling it to (4)_________ candidates. However, his decision was (5)_________ by the British parliament.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. raise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Raise money" is a standard, fixed collocation in English meaning to collect or generate funds, exactly the sense required here — the king wanted to generate more money to deal with the financial crisis.
◦ Example: The charity organised an event to raise money for flood victims.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: upraise — means to lift something physically upward (e.g., upraise one's arms); it is not used with "money" in the sense of generating funds.

• Option 3: bring — "bring money" would mean physically carrying money to a place, not generating/collecting it through taxes or other means, which is the intended sense here.

• Option 4: lift — like "upraise", this refers to physically lifting an object; "lift money" is not an established collocation for generating funds.

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations with "money" tested by SSC: raise money, save money, spend money, waste money, borrow money, launder money.

• Do not confuse "raise" (to increase/collect, transitive verb) with "rise" (to go up by itself, intransitive verb) — a very common SSC error-spotting trap.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The British king, Charles I, had (1)_________ a very difficult financial situation from his father. His period saw a very high rate of inflation. He wanted to (2)_________ money. Therefore, he (3)_________ creating the title of Baronet and selling it to (4)_________ candidates. However, his decision was (5)_________ by the British parliament.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. started.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes Charles I taking a new initiative to raise money — "creating the title of Baronet and selling it" — which is best introduced by "started", meaning to begin doing something new.
◦ Example: He started creating new titles to sell for extra income.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: ventured — usually means to dare to do something risky, often followed by "into" or "to" (e.g., "ventured into business"); "ventured creating" is not standard idiomatic usage.

• Option 3: continued — would wrongly imply that creating and selling the title of Baronet was already an existing, ongoing practice before this point, but the passage presents it as a new measure taken to solve the financial crisis.

• Option 4: appeared — "appeared creating" is grammatically incorrect; "appear" is normally followed by an infinitive ("appeared to create"), not a gerund, and does not fit the intended meaning of initiating an action.

NOTE

• Verbs like start, begin, commence are commonly followed directly by a gerund (V-ing) — "started creating", "began selling" — a pattern frequently tested in SSC cloze passages.

• "Venture" as a verb typically needs a preposition (venture into/on) or an infinitive (venture to do), and rarely takes a bare gerund object.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The British king, Charles I, had (1)_________ a very difficult financial situation from his father. His period saw a very high rate of inflation. He wanted to (2)_________ money. Therefore, he (3)_________ creating the title of Baronet and selling it to (4)_________ candidates. However, his decision was (5)_________ by the British parliament.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. wealthy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The king was selling the title of Baronet in order to raise money, so logically he would sell it to "wealthy" candidates — people who have enough money to pay a high price for the title.
◦ Example: The title was sold to wealthy candidates willing to pay a large sum.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: resourceful — means clever and skilled at finding quick solutions to problems; this describes a personal quality, not financial capacity to buy a title, so it does not fit the context of raising money.

• Option 2: opulent — is an adjective normally used to describe something lavish or luxurious (e.g., an opulent palace), not typically used to describe people ("opulent candidates" is not idiomatic).

• Option 3: healthy — refers to physical wellbeing, which is irrelevant to a person's ability to pay for a title.

NOTE

• When a cloze blank needs an adjective describing a type of "candidate/buyer" in a money-related context, look for words tied to financial capacity: wealthy, affluent, rich, well-off — as opposed to words describing personality, health, or general luxury of objects.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The British king, Charles I, had (1)_________ a very difficult financial situation from his father. His period saw a very high rate of inflation. He wanted to (2)_________ money. Therefore, he (3)_________ creating the title of Baronet and selling it to (4)_________ candidates. However, his decision was (5)_________ by the British parliament.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. rejected.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states that the British parliament did not approve of the king's decision to sell the title of Baronet — the natural word for a formal body refusing/turning down a decision is "rejected".
◦ Example: The proposal was rejected by the committee after a long debate.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: banished — means to send someone away from a place, usually as a punishment (e.g., banished from the kingdom); it applies to people being expelled, not to a decision being turned down.

• Option 3: unaccepted — this is not a standard/natural English word in formal usage; the conventional term for a proposal being turned down is "rejected", not "unaccepted".

• Option 4: abandoned — means to give up on something entirely or leave it incomplete, usually by the person who made the decision themselves; here it was the parliament (a separate body) that opposed the king's decision, so "rejected" (an external refusal) fits better than "abandoned" (self-initiated withdrawal).

NOTE

• Common words for a proposal/decision being turned down by an authority: rejected, vetoed, overruled, turned down, struck down.

• "Abandon" is more appropriate when the same person/party who started an action gives it up voluntarily, whereas "reject" describes another party disapproving of it.
